Token: The smallest unit of text a model works with — often a whole word, but sometimes a syllable, punctuation mark, or word fragment. Models read and write in tokens, not characters.
Tokenization: Splitting input text into tokens before the model can process it. A standardisation step that happens before any real understanding takes place.
Embedding: Mapping a token to a point in a high-dimensional mathematical space where meaning is encoded as position. Words with similar meanings end up close together, which is how a model 'knows' that dog and cat are more related than dog and bicycle.
Vector: An ordered list of numbers representing a token, word, or document as coordinates in embedding space. Similar meanings produce vectors that sit near each other.
Semantic search: Finding text by meaning rather than exact keywords, by comparing the embedding of a query against the embeddings of stored passages and returning the closest matches.
Neural network: The layered mathematical structure an LLM is built from. Input flows through layer after layer, each building a richer representation — early layers catch basic patterns, deeper layers grasp context and intent.
Transformer: The neural-network architecture behind modern LLMs. It stacks attention and feed-forward layers; an encoder processes the input sequence and a decoder generates output. GPT-style models are decoder-only.
Attention: The mechanism that lets a transformer link words that are far apart in a sentence, deciding which parts of the input are most relevant to each other when forming a response.
Generation: Producing output one token at a time. The model predicts the single most probable next token, appends it, and repeats — which is why LLMs can feel like they are 'thinking out loud'.
Inference: Running a trained model to produce output for new input. No learning happens at inference time — the model's weights are fixed; it only applies what it already learned.
LLM: Large Language Model — a neural network trained on vast amounts of text that learns patterns in language (grammar, facts, reasoning styles) and generates responses based on those learned patterns rather than looking things up.
GenAI: Generative AI — systems built around a large language model that produce new content (text, code, structured data) in response to a prompt and surrounding context.
Prompt: The input you give a model. In practice it is assembled into a fuller prompt context before generation begins.
Prompt context: Everything the model sees before it generates: the system prompt, the user's message, any retrieved documents, and any earlier tool results. Richer, more relevant context produces better output.
System prompt: Instructions that define how the model should behave — its persona, rules, and constraints. Sent in the system role, ahead of the user's message.
Role: A label on each message that tells the model what to treat as instructions, what to answer, and what is prior conversation. The three roles are system (persona and rules), user (input), and assistant (previous model responses).
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — keeping the base model frozen but supplying relevant context at inference time. The system embeds the question and a corpus, retrieves the most similar passages, and adds them to the prompt so the model can answer from your own data.
Knowledge source: An external database or document store a GenAI system searches (via RAG) to extend what the model knows beyond its training data.
Context window: The maximum number of tokens (system prompt + history + retrieved context + question) a model can attend to at once. When it fills, the oldest tokens drop out and the model loses access to them — large workflows split work into stages or use RAG to stay under the cap.
Temperature: A sampling control over randomness. Low values make output more deterministic and repeatable; higher values make it more varied and creative. Docs-grounded answers usually use a low temperature.
Greedy decoding: A sampling strategy that always picks the highest-probability next token. Deterministic and repeatable, but can be repetitive.
Top-k sampling: Restricting the next-token choice to the k most likely candidates, then sampling among them — a way to add controlled variety without picking implausible tokens.
Top-p sampling: Also called nucleus sampling. The next token is sampled from the smallest set of candidates whose combined probability exceeds p, adapting how many options are considered to the model's confidence.
Hallucination: When a model produces fluent but factually wrong or fabricated output. Grounding answers with RAG and citing sources reduces it.
Ollama: A tool for running open LLMs locally via a simple HTTP API (default http://localhost:11434). In this course Pentaho Data Integration calls Ollama so model inference stays on the VM and nothing leaves the box.
PDI: Pentaho Data Integration — the ETL platform used throughout this course as the orchestration layer that assembles inputs, calls the model, parses the response, and writes typed results back out.
Spoon: The desktop design tool for building and running Pentaho Data Integration transformations and jobs.
Transformation: A Pentaho Data Integration data-flow made of steps connected by hops, defined in a .ktr file. It moves and reshapes rows of data — including calling an LLM mid-flow.
Job: A Pentaho Data Integration orchestration unit (.kjb) that sequences transformations and other tasks, handling control flow, conditions, and error paths.
Orchestration: Pentaho Data Integration's role as the conductor: it gathers structured and unstructured inputs, hands them to the model with the right prompt, parses what comes back, and writes typed results to databases, files, or APIs.
Sentiment analysis: Classifying the emotional tone of text — positive, negative, or neutral — for example to score customer reviews. A common LLM-enrichment use case in Pentaho Data Integration.
Named Entity Recognition: Extracting named things from free text — people, organisations, places, dates — into structured fields. Handles reworded and paraphrased mentions that brittle regex rules would miss.
Data enrichment: Filling gaps the source data can't, by deriving new fields from free text — classification, language detection, intent labelling, country inference — using a model that understands meaning.
Data quality: Using a model to detect, flag, or correct problems in data — typos, inconsistencies, mis-categorisations — that rule-based checks struggle to catch.
Summarization: Condensing long text into a short, faithful summary as a pipeline step, so downstream stages or humans work with the gist instead of the full document.
Multi-stage pipeline: Decomposing a complex task into focused stages, each with a tight prompt. Errors are easier to localise and you can mix model sizes — a cheap classifier feeding an expensive synthesiser.
LangExtract: A lightweight approach (here, a REST service backed by Ollama) for turning free-form text into structured rows when regex is too brittle and full model training is too heavy.
Structured extraction: Pulling typed, schema-shaped fields out of unstructured text — support tickets, clinical notes, contracts — so the rest of an ETL flow can join, aggregate, and store them.
Schema: The declared shape of the data you want back — the fields and types an extraction service should produce. Centralising the schema in one service means upgrades roll out everywhere at once.
Agent: A system that reasons over intermediate output in a loop — calling the model, inspecting the result, fetching more data or calling a tool, then calling the model again — until it converges on an answer. A loop, not a single function call.
Agentic: Describing behaviour where the model can decide to act — call an API, run code, search — and feed the result back into its context to form its final answer.
Tool calling: Giving a model the ability to invoke external functions or APIs during a conversation. The result returns into the context and shapes the model's next step.
Agent-as-a-Service: Wrapping an agent behind a service endpoint so Pentaho Data Integration stays the orchestrator and many pipelines can call the same agent. Model swaps, prompt tweaks, and tool additions roll out once at the service.
Confidence threshold: A routing rule that trusts the model's answer when its certainty is high and escalates to a human (or a fallback) when it is low — scaling automation without sacrificing quality on edge cases.
Base64: A text encoding that represents binary data (such as an image) as ASCII characters, so it can be embedded in JSON payloads sent to or from a model API.
GenAI plugin suite: Twelve Pentaho Data Integration steps for generative AI: AI Chat, AI Chat Message Box, AI Segmentation, Text to Vector, Vector Writer, Vector Search, MCP Client, NER Extractor, Read Unstructured Document, Discover Metadata from Unstructured Documents, HTML Parser and Base64 Encoder. Every step needs a Pentaho license with GenAI (GENAI-EE) rights.
AI Chat: The GenAI step that sends each row's message, with a run instruction, to an LLM such as a local Ollama model, and adds the model's answer to the row. Its message comes from the dialog (Script) or from a field (Stream).
Run instruction: AI Chat's name for the system prompt: the instruction that tells the model how to behave and what to return, sent with every message.
Chunk: A piece of a longer text, small enough to embed or to fit a model's context window. AI Segmentation splits text into chunks, by paragraph, sentence, token count or a regular expression, with an optional overlap.
Vector store: A database that keeps embeddings with their text and metadata, and finds the stored vectors closest to a query vector. The course uses PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.
pgvector: The PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and similarity search. The course's lab kit runs it in the pcm-pgvector container on port 5433.
Cosine similarity: How closely two vectors point the same way, from -1 to 1. Vector Search turns it into a score from 0 to 1: (1 + cosine similarity) / 2.
Upsert: Insert a record, or replace it when a record with the same ID exists. Vector Writer upserts on its ID field, so a re-run does not duplicate the knowledge base.
MCP: The Model Context Protocol: a standard way for a server to offer tools and resources that a client, or a model through a client, can list and call. In PDI, the MCP Client step calls them directly and AI Chat's Tools tab lets the model choose.
Apache Tika: The open-source toolkit that detects a file's type and extracts its text and metadata. Read Unstructured Document and Discover Metadata from Unstructured Documents are built on it.
HNSW: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: the index pgvector builds to find the nearest vectors quickly without comparing the query with every row. Vector Writer does not create it; the RAG workshop creates it with CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw.
Chunk overlap: The text two neighboring chunks share, set in AI Segmentation. A little overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary whole in at least one chunk.
Top-k (retrieval): The number of closest matches Vector Search returns for each query vector, its Max results. Not to be confused with top-k sampling, which limits the tokens a model chooses from.
MCP server: A program that offers tools (actions with JSON arguments), and resources (readable data), over the Model Context Protocol. The MCP Tools workshop runs a small Python one over stdio.
stdio transport: An MCP connection that starts the server as a local process and talks to it over standard input and output. On Windows, start npx, uvx or python through cmd /c.
Streamable HTTP: The MCP transport for a server that runs as a web service; the connection names its URL. The older HTTP + SSE transport is not supported by the plugin.
Allowed tools: The list on an MCP connection that limits which of the server's tools PDI may call. Empty means all; listing only read-only tools keeps a model from calling one that changes data.
Run configuration: Where Spoon runs a transformation or job: Pentaho local (in Spoon itself) or a Pentaho Server. A run configuration named for the server sends the run to the server, which then needs the plugins, the license and the settings itself.
KETTLE_HOME: The folder that holds a PDI runtime's .kettle folder, and with it kettle.properties. Spoon, Carte and Pentaho Server can each have their own, which is why a variable set for Spoon may be missing on the server.
NER Extractor: The GenAI step that finds people, organizations, places, dates and numbers in text with Stanford CoreNLP, inside PDI: no LLM, no network, the same entities for the same text. It needs a larger Java heap and loads its models on the first row.
AI Segmentation: The GenAI step that splits a text field into chunks, one output row per chunk with its index, by paragraph, line, sentence, word, character, regular expression or recursively, sized in tokens or characters.
Map-reduce summary: Summarizing a document too long for one context window: summarize each chunk (map), then summarize the joined chunk summaries (reduce).
Vision model: A model that accepts images as well as text. In Ollama, ollama show lists its vision capability; the course uses gemma3:12b. AI Chat sends it an image attached from a file, a field, a URL or Base64.
LLM as judge: Using a second model, with a rubric, to grade a pipeline's answers: correct, partially correct, incorrect or correctly declined, and faithful to the passages or not.
Faithfulness: Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the passages the model was given. A judge can only measure it when it sees those passages.
Hit rate: The share of questions whose expected source document is among the retrieved passages: a measure of retrieval, before any answer is written.
Context recall: The share of an answer's expected facts that appear in the retrieved passages. Low context recall means the model cannot answer however good it is.
PII: Personally identifiable information: names, emails, phone numbers, account and card numbers, addresses. Mask it before text leaves the trusted zone.
Placeholder (masking): A typed stand-in such as [PERSON_1] or [EMAIL_1] that replaces a personal value in the text sent to a model, keeping the text readable while the value stays behind.
Luhn check: The checksum that valid card numbers pass. The masking step uses it to tell a card number from another long number, such as a tracking number.
Prompt injection: Text inside data, such as a customer message, that tries to give the model new instructions. The run instruction and validation of the answer limit it.
Carte: PDI's lightweight server, which runs transformations and jobs on request over a REST API. The Pentaho MCP Server project puts an MCP server in front of it.
Near-duplicate: Two records of the same real-world item that are not equal as text: reworded, misspelled, in other capitals or with an identifier written another way. Exact matching misses them; an embedding search finds them as close vectors.
Duplicate threshold: The lowest similarity score at which a pair of records is treated as a duplicate candidate. Chosen from measured scores, just below the lowest true duplicate, because look-alikes that are different items can score higher than true duplicates.
Hard negative: A record that scores close to another but is a different item, such as the same product in another size: the cases that show what a similarity threshold cannot separate.
Grounded generation: Generating text from given facts only, with the instruction forbidding anything else and a check downstream for what can be verified, such as numbers that do not appear in the source fields.
